messages.content:
A farmer must ferry a wolf, a goat, and a cabbage across a river.

- If left together **without the farmer**, the wolf eats the goat, and the
  goat eats the cabbage. (Nothing is ever eaten while the farmer is present,
  including in the boat.)
- The boat carries the farmer plus **up to two** of the three items.
- Every crossing of the river — in either direction, loaded or empty —
  counts as one crossing.

Read the constraints carefully; this is not quite the puzzle you may
remember. What is the **minimum total number of crossings** the farmer needs
to get all three items safely to the far side? Show the crossing plan, then
reply with the number.


When you are finished, output your final answer on its own line, as the last line of your response, in the exact format:
ANSWER: <your answer>

text:
The boat's capacity of farmer + at most two items immediately rules out a solution in a single crossing. After any even number of crossings the farmer is on the near bank, so it is impossible for all three items to be on the far bank (they would be unsupervised and the goat would be eaten). Hence at least three crossings are required.

The following three-crossing schedule meets the capacity limit and never leaves an unsupervised wolf-goat or goat-cabbage pair:

- Crossing 1: farmer takes wolf and cabbage to the far bank  
  (near bank: goat; far bank: farmer, wolf, cabbage).  
- Crossing 2: farmer returns alone  
  (near bank: farmer, goat; far bank: wolf, cabbage).  
- Crossing 3: farmer takes goat to the far bank  
  (near bank: empty; far bank: farmer, wolf, goat, cabbage).

All three items are now safely on the far side.

ANSWER: 3
